title: Build with Make
summary: Write a Makefile with warnings, a clean target, and correct dependencies.

scenario.briefing: A C utility builds by hand on one laptop and silently ignores warnings. Turn the build into a Makefile that recompiles changed inputs, fails on warnings, and cleans its output.

objectives.description: Write a Makefile with warnings and a phony clean target.
Predict what make rebuilds after one file changes.
Explain Make dependencies and flags accurately.

hints: Declare the compiler and flags as variables.
Declare .PHONY: clean so clean always runs.
The app target depends on main.c and compiles it with $(CC) $(CFLAGS).

misconceptions.testDescription: Warnings are part of every compile.
misconceptions.feedback: A build that ignores warnings hides real defects. Put the warning flags in CFLAGS so every compile uses them.

misconceptions.description: Believing make rebuilds every target after any change.
misconceptions.feedback: make compares timestamps. Changing main.c rebuilds app, but clean is not part of that dependency chain.
Warnings catch some defects at compile time. They do not prove behavior; tests still exercise the program.

sections.title: A Makefile is a dependency graph
sections.body: Each target lists prerequisites and a recipe. make rebuilds a target when a prerequisite is newer than the target. That timestamp rule is why incremental builds are fast and why a missing prerequisite produces stale binaries.

sections.title: Warnings belong in the build
sections.body: Flags such as -Wall, -Wextra, and -Werror turn compiler diagnostics into build failures. A warning that never fails the build is easy to ignore until it becomes a production bug. Keep the flags in CFLAGS so every compile uses them.

sections.title: Phony targets are commands, not files
sections.body: A target such as clean does not produce a file named clean. Declaring it .PHONY prevents make from skipping the recipe when a file with that name exists. The same rule applies to test, format, and other command targets.

vocabulary.definition: A build output or command name in a Makefile.
A file or target that must be up to date before a target runs.
A target that always runs because it does not represent a file.
Rebuilding only the outputs whose inputs changed.

steps.title: Write the Makefile
steps.prompt: Edit Makefile. Build app from main.c with cc, -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror, and a phony clean target that removes app.

files.content:
CC = cc
CFLAGS = -std=c17
TARGET = app

# TODO: enable warnings and mark clean phony
app: main.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) main.c -o $(TARGET)

clean:
	rm -f $(TARGET)

localVerification.description: Clean and build the app with Make.

steps.title: Predict the rebuild
steps.prompt: You run make after editing only main.c. What does make rebuild?

options.label: app, because main.c is newer than app
Nothing, because the Makefile did not change

quiz.explanation: make rebuilds app because its prerequisite main.c changed. clean is not a prerequisite of app and does not run unless requested.

hints: Only targets that depend on the changed file are rebuilt.
clean is not in app's dependency chain.

steps.title: Targets, flags, and dependencies

statements.label: A phony target always runs its recipe.
make uses file timestamps to decide what is out of date.
Compiler warnings replace the need for tests.
The clean target should remove generated build outputs.

steps.explanation: Make is driven by dependencies and timestamps. Phony targets such as clean are commands, and warning flags complement tests rather than replacing them.
hints: clean should leave no generated binary behind.
